messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Michael's Case

Michael was fifty-eight when he came to his first appointment, and he arrived fifteen minutes early to the clinic—not out of conscientiousness, but because he needed time to assess the waiting room. He sat in the corner chair that faced the door and the reception desk, his back against the wall. From there, he could see anyone who entered. He had learned to choose his seats this way everywhere: restaurants, his dental practice, his partner's house when they had people over. The habit had formed so gradually that he no longer consciously registered the calculation; it was simply what he did now.

Three years earlier, Michael had been closing his practice on a Thursday evening in late October when two officers came through the door. He was alone, finishing paperwork in his office. What happened in the next forty minutes had fractured something in him that he could not quite name. The officers claimed he matched a description from an armed robbery at a convenience store six blocks away. He had not been there. He had been at his practice. But in those moments—when they forced him against the wall, when one of them drove his face into the carpeted floor, when they restrained his arms and the pressure on his chest made him certain he could not breathe—Michael had not been thinking about innocence or facts. He had been thinking only that he was going to die, that no one knew he was there, that his body was being destroyed.

He was released within two hours after they checked the store's security footage. There was an apology, brief and perfunctory. No charges. No follow-up. No acknowledgment of the bruises on his ribs or the small cut on his forehead. The case went nowhere. The officers were never disciplined. Michael had come to believe that what happened to him was not only terrifying but fundamentally unjust—that he had been marked by something random and cruel, and that the world had decided it did not matter.

In the months that followed, Michael noticed he could not sleep through the night. He would fall asleep around eleven, then wake at two or three, his heart racing, sometimes hearing the officers' voices—the particular cadence of their commands, the scrape of their boots on the floor. These sounds were not memories in any way he could understand them; they arrived in his head as though someone had pressed play on a recording. When they came, he also felt a sharp ache in his shoulders and neck, the exact places where hands had gripped him. It was as though his body was remembering something his mind was trying to distance itself from.

What made it stranger still was that the memory itself felt like it belonged to someone else. When he tried to think about what happened, it was like watching a film of a stranger's assault. He could see it happening, but he could not quite connect it to himself, Michael, the man who had built a successful practice, who had been with his partner Richard for twelve years. That disconnection frightened him more than the memory itself.

He began to avoid anything that might disturb him. He stopped listening to music in the car because a song might trigger something. He declined invitations from friends. He stopped going to the grocery store at certain times because he did not want to encounter unfamiliar people in close quarters. A stranger approaching him on the street—even someone asking for directions—made his body tense, his mind certain that threat was imminent. He found himself constantly scanning his environment, cataloging exits, assessing the intentions of people around him. At his practice, he started scheduling only patients he knew, turning away new referrals. His income began to decline.

Richard had noticed the changes. Michael was emotionally distant, rarely present even when they were together. He would not go out to dinner anymore. He had stopped laughing. When Richard tried to comfort him, Michael would stiffen, unable to tolerate the closeness. Richard had suggested therapy months ago, but Michael had resisted. He was certain that talking about it would only make it worse, that dwelling on what happened would destroy him further. But the isolation was becoming unbearable. He was not living; he was hiding. And he was no longer sure he could hide well enough to keep himself safe.
